noi_dung:
When Deluded, the Master Saves; When Enlightened, Save Yourself

Now is Chan Session time (December 15, 1977). Raise up the hua-tou to investigate, applying effort hour after hour, minute after minute. Cultivators must cultivate by themselves—never leaning on others, still less leaning on their own teacher. At the Session, we cultivate—not our teacher—see this clearly. Someone thinks: "While the Master is at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, I apply effort; when the Master is away, I needn't strive." Thinking so will not do. Whether the teacher is at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas or not, we still strive vigorously in cultivation—thorough before and after—only then is there hope of accomplishment. Otherwise you merely cultivate outwardly—deceiving yourselves and others—never to be liberated.

Investigating the hua-tou means investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—asking who is reciting the Buddha's name. Saying: "I am reciting the Buddha's name"—then when I die, where does this "I" run off to? Clearly not this "I." Investigating so, no "I" can be found. If there is no "I," then while alive need we cultivate at all? Thinking so is also wrong. Then what is right? Investigate our original face (the fundamental face)—what was it before our parents gave birth to us? Investigate penetratingly—and you will become enlightened.

Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Pursue it hour after hour, minute after minute, second after second, unrelenting. In fact this is the skill of countering poison with poison. Who recites the Buddha's name? Though it too is a thought, take one thought to control all other thoughts—take one discursive thought to halt all discursive thoughts. Halting to the extreme, the moment comes when waters recede and rocks appear, true features show, and you are enlightened.

What is enlightenment? Truly seeing what you are, realizing the principle of emptiness, understanding all is hollow—and that is true understanding. Then you know what state "Fundamentally not a single thing—where can dust alight?" is. That too is the state of understanding the mind and seeing the nature. There is a saying, "With the mind understood, nothing is hard; with the nature seen, sorrow unknown"—meaning that reaching mind-understanding, whatever befalls brings no sorrow. Another saying goes:

Since ancient times, immortals have no special magic;

Vastly giving rise to joy, giving rise to no sorrow.

This means immortals of old had nothing unusual—for giving rise to vast joy, they had no sorrow. That marks those who cultivate the Way.

Whoever cultivates the Way—meeting adverse or favorable states, the mind stays unmoved. With samadhi power at that level, states no longer shake you—instead you can turn states around. That is the true skill of the cultivator of the Way. Another saying:

Mount Tai crumbling before you, unstartled;

Beauty before your eyes, unmoved.

A rough translation:

Mount Tai collapsing, yet unafraid;

Beauty before your eyes, the mind unmoved.

A young man before a beauty like Xi Shi, say—contemplating the "skull," his mind naturally stills. A young woman meeting a handsome youth like Pan An of old—contemplating "white bones," likewise unmoved. Without that dharma, meeting pretty girls or handsome boys, the mind scampers—like gibbons climbing, like horses galloping—never knowing what is right. Only through samadhi power too weak—and so the Way-karma wasted in vain. How regrettable!

Today I received a letter from two pilgrims on the "three steps, one bow" journey, and I understand the inconceivable things they have just been through, sheltered by dragon spirits and Dharma protectors. "Sympathetic response in the Way" is just this. Those two bowed sincerely, recited truly—moving the heavenly dragons of the eightfold division to ever stand beside them guarding. So wherever they go, all goes smoothly—peril turned to safety. Take them as bright mirrors, reflecting on yourselves—are you so pure? So clear, so wise, so free of discursive thoughts?

Friends! Hearing Sutras and Dharma, you must awaken to your own nature—awaken yourselves and save yourselves. You cannot lean on the Master! You must rely on yourselves. It is said, "The master leads you to the gate; practice is your own affair." Trust your own wisdom—never trust your own delusion. This point is of utmost weight. We join the Session aiming that our own natures save themselves. Of old the Sixth Patriarch said: "When deluded, the master saves; when enlightened, save yourself."

Now as we investigate Chan, use every second—wasting no time. Hence during Chan investigation we do not bow to the Buddhas, take formal meals, or make noon offerings—why? To help you focus on effort. One more minute investigating—enlightenment's chance one minute nearer. Where is spare time for other things—for chatter, for gathering? Clustering in twos and threes, gossiping rights and wrongs—all meaningless—truly squandering enlightenment's chance. Though you investigated for eighty thousand great kalpas, no hope at all. In the Session, investigate honestly! Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigate "What was my original face before my parents gave birth to me?" That is wisdom's key.

In Chan Investigation, Conquer the "Gate of Pain"

Today, the New Year, I wish you a "Happy New Year." Such is worldly custom. We world-leavers should not follow that custom—yet we remain people in the world; too far from the world, we leave people behind. So I follow custom, wishing everyone "a happy new year." I add this verse:

Now meets the year nineteen-eighty-two;

From ten directions gather to investigate Chan.

Returning the light, contemplating at ease;

In the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, sages are selected.

A rough translation:

This year, nineteen-eighty-two;

Gathered at Ten Thousand Buddhas to investigate Chan.

Returning the light, contemplating at ease;

Right here, sages are selected.

A happy New Year! For us Chan investigators, we must reach "taking Chan bliss as food"—the true Chan investigator, eaten or not, does not remember; dressed or not, slept or not, does not remember. Investigating to the ultimate—above, no sky known; below, no earth known; between, no people seen—merged into one with empty space, dwelling in a state of no others, no self, no beings, no life. In that state, aching legs matter nothing—aching back, no fear—for patient effort carries the meditator past all. For with no people, no self, no beings, no life—who is it that aches? Moreover, past the "gate of pain," pain passes too; unpassed, pain remains. Past the gate of pain, the meditator is not only pain-free but at ease, joyful beyond measure.

No Dharma-door is more wondrous than Chan investigation—for Chan investigation alone leads to taking Chan bliss as food, replete with Dharma joy. Hence since ancient times Chan adepts could sit days on end without rising. Did their legs ache? Of course they ached! But they could bear pain—bearing what others cannot bear. With valiant, vigorous energy, knowing only to press forward, never to retreat—and so they succeeded.

Chan investigation demands patience—for patience is enlightenment's capital. Like merchants in trade—capital is needed for business to grow and profit much. In Chan investigation we must conquer the gate of pain; past the gate of pain, the road opens bright and wide, leading straight to understanding the mind and seeing the nature. Unpassed this barrier, still "mountains ending, waters exhausted, the road blocked"—passed, it is "beneath the willows, bright flowers—another village." There are sayings:

Unable to cast off death, no life gained;

Unable to cast off the false, no truth realized;

Unable to cast off suffering, no bliss attained.

In Chan investigation we must hold such a spirit to hope for success. Smash through hardship's gate to see another (true) state. Hence we must be single in Chan investigation. Take heed! We come here to investigate Chan—not to kill time. Bring forth your truest resolve to apply effort, with truest patience to sit in Chan. Remember one thing: in this world, nothing is reaped without labor. Reaping without sowing—can things be so easy? That is hollow dreaming, never real. Only your own strength given promises the day of accomplishment. Now, the New Year come, you hold new hopes—hoping this year for enlightenment. May we all press toward this goal—unenlightened, never halting.

Talks at the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall, City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Chan Session, January 1 to 8, 1982.
